t.5.1: Her hopes shattered by Pinākin, who had thus burned Manobhava before her very eyes, Pārvatī reproached her own beauty in her heart; for loveliness finds its fruit in being cherished by those one loves.
t.5.3: And Menā, hearing that her daughter, whose heart was fixed upon Girīśa, had resolved to undertake austerities, clasped her to her breast and spoke, trying to hold her back from the great vow of an ascetic.
t.5.2: She resolved to make her own beauty bear fruit by taking up deep meditation through austerities; for how else could that twofold prize be won, a love of such a kind and a husband such as he?
t.5.4: The gods you long for are present even in your home, my child; how far apart are austerity and this body of yours! A śirīṣa flower can bear the delicate foot of a bee, but never that of a bird.
t.5.5: Though she counseled her daughter thus, Menā could not restrain her, whose wish was firm, from her resolve; for who could turn back a mind steadfastly set upon its desired aim, or water flowing toward low ground?
t.5.6: Once, speaking through the mouth of a close friend, the resolute maiden asked her father, who already knew her heart's desire, that she be allowed to dwell in the forest, for ascetic meditation that would last until its fruit was attained.
t.5.7: Then, granted leave by her most venerable father, who was pleased by her fitting resolve, Gaurī went to a peak frequented by peacocks, which afterwards became famous among the people by her name.
t.5.9: Just as her face had been lovely with her well-adorned tresses, so it was even with matted locks; a lotus shines not only with rows of bees but also when entangled with moss.
t.5.8: Firm in a resolve that nothing could shake, she cast off her necklace, whose swaying strands had rubbed away her sandal paste, and the young girl bound on a reddish-brown garment of bark, its close-knit fibres torn apart by the swell of her breasts.
t.5.10: The triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass that she wore for her vow, which made her body-hair bristle at every moment, was bound on her then for the first time, and by it the place where her girdle-string rested was made red.
t.5.11: Withdrawn from her lip, which had given up its red dye, and from the ball reddened by the cosmetic paint of her breasts, her hand, its fingers wounded from plucking sprouts of kuśa grass, was made by her a devoted companion of the rosary.
t.5.12: She who used to be pained even by the flowers of her own hair that fell as she turned on a costly bed now slept on the bare ground itself, having sunk down upon it with only her creeper-like arm for a pillow.
t.5.13: While she kept her vow, she placed two things in two keepers, as if in trust, to take them back again: her graceful movements in the slender creepers, and her tremulous glances in the does.
t.5.15: Fondled and fed by her with handfuls of wild grain, the deer came to trust her so fully that, out of curiosity, she measured her own eyes against theirs in front of her friends.
t.5.14: Unwearied, she herself nurtured the young trees with streams poured from her water-pots as if from breasts; even Guha will not take away her motherly love for these, who were the first to be born to her.
t.5.16: Eager to see her, the seers came to her as she, having performed her ritual bath and made offerings to Jātavedas, sat wearing an upper garment of bark and devoted to sacred study; for among those grown great in dharma, age is not taken into account.
t.5.17: That grove of austerities, too, became purifying: there creatures hostile by nature had cast off their former enmity, guests were honored by the trees with the fruits they desired, and fire was kept burning within new huts of leaves.
t.5.18: When she judged that the fruit she longed for could not be won by her earlier ascetic meditation, which had gone only so far, she then disregarded the tenderness of her own body and set out to practise great austerity.
t.5.19: She who grew weary even from playing with a ball plunged into the austere life of the sages. Surely her body was fashioned of golden lotuses, soft by nature and yet full of firm strength.
t.5.20: In the hot season, the slender-waisted one of radiant smile, standing in the midst of four blazing fires, overcame the glare that repels the eyes and gazed at the sun with unwavering sight.
t.5.21: Though thus scorched by the rays of the sun, her face bore the beauty of a lotus; only at its long outer corners of the eyes did a dark shadow slowly, slowly gain a foothold.
t.5.22: Only water that came unbidden, and the rays of the moon, lord of the stars, whose very nature is nectar: such, they say, was her breaking of the fast, its means no different from the way trees sustain themselves.
t.5.24: The first drops of rain rested a moment on her eyelashes, then struck her lower lip; shattered by their fall upon the high swell of her breasts, they stumbled down the folds of her waist and only after a long while reached her navel.
t.5.23: Intensely scorched by fire of different kinds, the one that roams the sky and the one fed with heaped-up fuel, she, when the hot season ended and she was sprinkled with fresh rains, released, together with the earth, an upward-rising breath of heat.
t.5.25: The nights, standing as though witnesses to her great austerity, gazed upon her as she lay on the bare rock with no roof to dwell under, through the unbroken rains lashed by wind, with their opening eyes of lightning.
t.5.26: Intent on dwelling in water, she passed the nights of Sahasya, whose winds scattered bitter frost, full of pity for the pair of cakravāka birds before her, parted from each other and crying out to one another.
t.5.27: At night she, trembling, with her face fragrant as a lotus and lovely with its petal-like lower lip, seemed to restore a lotus to the waters, whose wealth of lotuses had been ruined by the falling frost.
t.5.28: For living on leaves that have fallen from the trees of their own accord is the highest limit of austerity; yet even that she cast aside, and therefore those who know the ancient lore call her, the sweet-spoken one, Aparṇā, the leafless.
t.5.29: Day and night wearing down, by vows such as these, her own body, soft as a slender lotus stalk, she cast far below her the austerity that ascetics had won with their hardened bodies.
t.5.30: Then into the penance-grove there entered a certain ascetic with matted locks, wearing a deerskin and bearing a staff of palāśa wood, bold of speech and seeming to blaze with a splendour born of Brahman, like the first stage of life, the student's stage, embodied in human form.
t.5.31: The hospitable Pārvatī went forth to meet him with worship marked by great respect. Even where there is equality, the actions of those whose minds are steadfast are deeply reverent toward persons of distinguished form.
t.5.32: Having accepted the hospitality offered according to rule and rested for a moment, ostensibly to shake off his weariness, he looked at Umā with a straight and honest gaze and began to speak, never departing from due decorum.
t.5.33: Are kindling and kuśa grass easy for you to obtain for your rites? Are the waters fit for the ritual of bathing? Do you practise austerity according to your own strength? For the body, indeed, is the first means of fulfilling dharma.
t.5.34: Is the tender shoot of these creepers, nourished by the water you have poured out for them, still flourishing, that shoot which rises to equal your lip, rosy even though it long ago gave up its lac?
t.5.35: Is your heart kindly disposed toward the deer, who fondly snatch the darbha grass from your hand, and who, O lotus-eyed one, seem with their restless eyes to imitate the likeness of your own eyes?
t.5.36: What is said, O Pārvatī, that beauty does not lend itself to sinful conduct, is a saying that never fails; for indeed your character, dwelling in so noble a form, has become a lesson even for ascetics.
t.5.37: This mountain, together with his whole lineage, has been purified not so much by the waters of the Gaṅgā fallen from heaven, laughing bright with the scattered offerings of the Seven Sages, as by your own spotless deeds.
t.5.38: By this, O noble lady, dharma today appears to me all the more to be the essence of the three aims of life, since you, whose mind has turned away from wealth and desire, have embraced dharma alone and devote yourself to it.
t.5.39: You ought not to regard me as a stranger, me on whom you yourself have bestowed such special hospitality; for, O you of gracefully bowed limbs, the wise declare that the friendship of the good is sealed in just seven steps.
t.5.40: Therefore, O lady rich in austerities, this person here, prone to rashness by reason of his being a twice-born, wishes to ask you, who are so forbearing, something on this matter; if it is no secret, you ought to answer.
t.5.41: Birth in the family of the first Creator, a body like the beauty of the three worlds risen into form, the joy of sovereignty that need not be sought, and fresh youth: tell me, what fruit of austerity could there be beyond this?
t.5.42: Such a resolve in proud-spirited women arises, it is said, from something unwelcome and hard to bear; yet even when I send my mind along the paths of reflection, O slender-waisted one, no such thing can be seen in you.
t.5.43: This form of yours is one that grief cannot overcome; how could there be any humiliation in your father's house, O fair-browed one? Nor can there be an assault on you by another, for who would stretch out his hand toward the jewel-point on a serpent's head?
t.5.44: Why, casting off your ornaments in the prime of youth, have you put on this bark garment that befits old age? Tell me: when evening has just fallen and the moon and stars shine bright, does the night ever hasten toward the dawn?
t.5.45: If you seek heaven, your toil is in vain, for your father's regions are themselves the lands of the gods; and if you seek a husband, enough of this meditation, for a jewel does not go searching, it is the one that is sought.
t.5.46: Your warm sigh has made it known, yet my mind only plunges into doubt: no one is seen who would be worthy of your seeking, so how could one sought by you be hard to win?
t.5.47: Ah, how hard-hearted is that young man you desire, whoever he may be, who looks on unmoved at your matted locks, tawny as the tips of kalama rice, hanging loosely on your cheek, which has long been bare of its ear-lotus!
t.5.48: Seeing you so excessively wasted by the vows of a sage, the places where your ornaments once lay scorched by the sun, like a sliver of the moon seen by day, whose mind, if he has any feeling at all, is not pained?
t.5.50: How long will you go on wearying yourself, Gaurī? I too have austerity gathered in my earlier stage of life; with half a share of it, obtain the bridegroom you long for, and I wish to know him well.
t.5.49: I take it that your beloved has been led astray by pride in his good fortune, since he does not long make his own face the target of this charmingly glancing eye of yours with its curving lashes.
t.5.51: Thus addressed by the twice-born one, who had probed so deeply, she could not bring herself to speak what lay in her mind. Then, turning her eye, bare of collyrium, she looked at the friend who stood at her side.
t.5.52: Her friend said to the student: "Hear, good sir, if you are curious, the reason for which she has made her body an instrument of austerity, as one might make a lotus into a shade against the heat."
t.5.53: This proud maiden, disdaining the lords of the four quarters, great Indra and the rest, who hold sway over fortune, wishes to win as her husband the Pināka-bearer, who since his subduing of Madana cannot be won by beauty.
t.5.54: The arrow of the flower-bowed Kāma, which long ago was turned back by Purāri's unbearable roar of 'huṃ' and never reached its mark in him, has struck this girl deep in the heart, even though the archer's body has been destroyed.
t.5.55: From that time on, maddened by love in her father's house, her locks grey with the sandal paste of her forehead mark, the girl never found relief, not even on slabs of rock formed of packed ice.
t.5.56: When the deeds of the Pināka-bearer were taken up in song, she, with words faltering in a throat choked with tears, many a time moved to weeping the daughters of the Kiṃnara king, her companions in singing at the forest's edge.
t.5.57: And on nights when only a third remained, she would close her eyes for a moment and then suddenly wake, crying out to one unseen, “Where are you going, Nīlakaṇṭha?”, her arms clasped around a neck that was not there.
t.5.59: And when, searching for a means, she saw no other way of winning him, the Lord of the world, then, with the permission of her elder, she came with us to this grove of penance to practise austerities.
t.5.58: "When the wise proclaim you all-pervading, how is it that you do not know this person whose heart is fixed on you?" Thus, in secret, the innocent girl reproached Candraśekhara, whom she had drawn with her own hand.
t.5.60: Even on these trees, which my friend herself planted and which have witnessed her austerities, fruit has been seen; yet her heart's desire, which rests upon the moon-crested god, is not seen even on the verge of sprouting.
t.5.61: I do not know when he, so earnestly sought and so hard to win, will come to favor this friend of ours, wasted by austerities and gazed upon by her companions through their tears, as the rain-god comes to the furrow scorched by his own withholding of rain.
t.5.62: Thus told of Umā's unconcealed true feeling by her friend, who could read gestures, the handsome lifelong celibate, betraying no sign of his joy, asked Umā: "Ah, is this really so, or is it a jest?"
t.5.63: Then the daughter of the Mountain, placing her small crystal rosary in the forepart of her hand, its fingers folded like a bud, spoke with difficulty in measured syllables, her speech having long been held in check.
t.5.64: O best of those who know the Veda, it is as you have heard: this person is eager to rise to a lofty station, and this austerity, they say, is the means of attaining it. For desires there is nothing beyond reach.
t.5.65: Then the student said: "Maheśvara is well known, and yet you still long for him. Considering him, who delights in the constant practice of inauspicious things, I cannot bring myself to go along with you."
t.5.67: Consider this yourself, just for a moment: could these two ever be fit to be joined, a bride's silken garment marked with figures of kalahaṃsa geese, and an elephant's hide raining drops of blood?
t.5.66: Set as you are on so worthless an attachment, how will this hand of yours, bound with the wedding thread, endure that first clasp of Śambhu's hand, on which a snake is coiled as a bracelet?
t.5.68: Who, even an enemy, would ever consent that your two feet, fit for a courtyard strewn with heaps of flowers, should leave their lac-dyed footprints on cremation grounds strewn with the hair of the dead?
t.5.69: Tell me, what could be more unfitting than this: that even if the chest of the Three-eyed One is easily won by you, the dust of funeral-pyre ash will set its mark upon this pair of breasts, the resting place of yellow sandal paste?
t.5.70: And here is yet another mockery awaiting you: when the great crowd sees the old bull mounted by you, a newly wedded bride worthy to be carried by a lordly elephant, their faces will break into smiles.
t.5.71: Through longing for union with Kapālin, two things have now become pitiable: that lustrous digit of the moon, and you, the moonlight for the eyes of this world.
t.5.72: His body has misshapen eyes, his birth is unknown, and his wealth is proclaimed by his going sky-clad. O young fawn-eyed one, of all that is sought in bridegrooms, is even a single thing to be found in Trilocana?
t.5.73: Turn your mind away from this unworthy desire: where is one such as he, and where are you, who bear auspicious marks? Good people do not expect the Vedic honor due to a sacrificial post to be paid to a stake in the cremation ground.
t.5.74: When the twice-born spoke thus against her wishes, she, her anger betrayed by her trembling lower lip, cast her eyes upon him sidelong, their corners reddened, the creepers of her brows knit in a frown.
t.5.75: And she said to him: "Surely you do not know Hara in his true nature, since you speak to me in this way; the dull-witted despise the conduct of the great-souled, which is unlike that of ordinary folk and whose motives are beyond conception."
t.5.77: Though himself possessing nothing, he is the source of all riches; though he haunts the abode of the dead, he is lord of the three worlds; though terrible in form, he is called Śiva, the auspicious. There are none who know the true nature of the Bearer of Pināka.
t.5.76: The auspicious is pursued by one intent on warding off calamity, or by one eager for prosperity; but what has he, the refuge of the world, who is free of all desire, to do with these, whose very nature is marred by longing?
t.5.79: Having gained contact with his body, the dust of funeral-pyre ash surely serves for purification; for indeed, when it falls from him in the course of his dance and gestures, it is smeared upon the crowned heads of the sky-dwellers.
t.5.78: Whether it shines with ornaments or is bound with serpents, whether it is draped in an elephant's hide or clad in fine silk, whether it bears a skull or is crested with the moon, the body of him whose form is the universe cannot be fixed.
t.5.80: Though he is without wealth and goes about on a bull, Vṛṣā, whose mount is the rutting elephant of the quarters, approaches him and, bowing with his crown, makes his feet red-toed with the pollen of the full-blown mandāra flowers.
t.5.81: Though you, of fallen mind, meant to speak only fault, you have said one thing rightly about the Lord: he whom even the self-born ones proclaim to be the cause, how could his origin ever be known?
t.5.82: Enough of argument; let him be entirely such as you have heard him to be. My mind rests fixed on him, its one delight in devotion, and one who acts as love moves does not heed reproach.
t.5.83: Friend, let this young brahmin be stopped somehow, for he wishes to speak again, his upper and lower lips quivering. Not only he who speaks ill of the great, but he too who listens to him, becomes a partaker of sin.
t.5.84: Saying, "Or rather, I shall go away from here," the maiden started to move, her bark garment parting at her breasts; and he whose banner bears the king of bulls, resuming his own form and smiling, caught hold of her.
t.5.85: Seeing him, the daughter of the king of mountains, trembling, her slender body moist with sweat, holding up the foot she had lifted to set down, neither went on nor stayed, like a river thrown into turmoil by a mountain blocking its path.
t.5.86: When the moon-crested god said, “From this day on, O you of bowed limbs, I am your slave, bought by your austerities,” she at once cast off the weariness born of her vows; for hardship, through its fruit, brings back freshness anew.
